**Rick Douglas Husband** (July 12, 1957– February 1, 2003) was an American [astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut") and [fighter pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighter_pilot "Fighter pilot"). He traveled into space twice: as pilot of [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96") and commander of [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"). Husband and the rest of the crew of STS-107 were killed when _Columbia_[disintegrated during reentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") into the [Earth's atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere"). He is also a recipient of the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").

## Early life, education and training

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life, education and training")]

Husband was born on July 12, 1957, in [Amarillo, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amarillo,_Texas "Amarillo, Texas").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-NASA_Bio-1) At age 17, he earned his pilot's license while flying out of [Tradewind Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tradewind_Airport "Tradewind Airport"). Husband graduated with honors from [Amarillo High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amarillo_High_School "Amarillo High School") in 1975.

Husband earned a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [mechanical engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanical_engineering "Mechanical engineering") from [Texas Tech University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Tech_University "Texas Tech University") in 1980 after five years of study. He earned his [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree from [Fresno State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresno_State_University "Fresno State University"). Upon graduation, Husband was commissioned as a pilot in the [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force"), having been enrolled in [ROTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ROTC "ROTC") his last two years of college. Husband underwent pilot training at [Vance Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vance_Air_Force_Base "Vance Air Force Base"), in [Enid, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enid,_Oklahoma "Enid, Oklahoma"). This was followed by Land Survival School at [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base"), in [Spokane, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington"), and [Fighter Lead-in School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trainer_aircraft#Lead-in_fighter_training "Trainer aircraft") in New Mexico. After he got married on February 27, 1982, Husband trained in the [F-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-4 "F-4") at [Homestead Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homestead_Air_Force_Base "Homestead Air Force Base") next.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-Rick-2)

## U.S. Air Force career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: U.S. Air Force career")]

Husband was assigned to a squadron at [Moody Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Air_Force_Base "Moody Air Force Base") in [Valdosta, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valdosta,_Georgia "Valdosta, Georgia"), flying the F-4E. He then transferred to [George AFB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_AFB "George AFB"), in [Victorville, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorville,_California "Victorville, California") in December 1985, where Husband became an F-4 instructor. By then, he had accumulated 1000 hours of flying time.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-Rick-2):30,32

In December 1987, Husband was assigned to [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), where he attended the [USAF Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USAF_Test_Pilot_School "USAF Test Pilot School") class 88A along with future [Canadian Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Space_Agency "Canadian Space Agency") astronaut [Chris Hadfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hadfield "Chris Hadfield"). Upon completion of test pilot school, Husband served as a test pilot flying the F-4 and all five models of the [F-15 Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-15_Eagle "F-15 Eagle"). In the F-15 Combined Test Force, he was the program manager for the [Pratt & Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratt_&_Whitney "Pratt & Whitney")[F100-PW-229](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratt_&_Whitney_F100#F100-PW-229 "Pratt & Whitney F100") increased performance engine and also served as the F-15 Aerial Demonstration Pilot.

In June 1992, Husband was assigned to the Aircraft and Armament Evaluation Establishment at [Boscombe Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boscombe_Down "Boscombe Down"), England, as an exchange test pilot with the [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force"). At Boscombe Down, he was the Tornado GR1 and GR4 Project Pilot and served as a test pilot in the Hawk, Hunter, Buccaneer, Jet Provost, Tucano, and Harvard.

Husband logged over 3,800 hours of flight time in more than 40 different types of [aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft "Aircraft").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-NASA_Bio-1)

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Husband was selected as an astronaut candidate by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") in December 1994, the same week he was promoted to lieutenant colonel.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-Rick-2):67 Husband reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in March 1995 to begin a year of training and evaluation. Upon completion of training, he was named the Astronaut Office representative for Advanced Projects at Johnson Space Center, working on [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") Upgrades, the [Crew Return Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew_Return_Vehicle "Crew Return Vehicle") (CRV) and studies to return to the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon") and travel to [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"). Husband eventually served as Chief of Safety for the [Astronaut Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_Office "Astronaut Office"). In 1999, he flew as pilot on [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96") and logged 235 hours and 13 minutes in [space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_space "Outer space"). Husband was later assigned to command the crew of [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), which was launched early in 2003. Along with the rest of the STS-107 crew, he was killed upon reentry when the shuttle disintegrated over Texas.

## Shuttle missions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Shuttle missions")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/STS-96_Rick_Husband_and_Tamara_Jernigan.jpg/250px-STS-96_Rick_Husband_and_Tamara_Jernigan.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-96_Rick_Husband_and_Tamara_Jernigan.jpg)

Pilot (PLT) Rick D. Husband (left) and EVA Specialist [Tamara E. Jernigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamara_E._Jernigan "Tamara E. Jernigan") (right) during STS-96

*   [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96") (May 27 to June 6, 1999) aboard the [Space Shuttle _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery") was a 10-day mission during which the crew performed the first docking with the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") and delivered four tons of logistics and supplies in preparation for the arrival of the [first crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_1 "Expedition 1") to live on the station early the following year. The mission was accomplished in 153 Earth orbits, traveling 4 million miles in 9 days, 19 hours and 13 minutes.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Commander_%28CDR%29_Rick_D._Husband_%28left%29_and_Payload_Specialist_%28PS%29_Ilan_Ramon_%28right%29_during_STS-107.jpg/250px-Commander_%28CDR%29_Rick_D._Husband_%28left%29_and_Payload_Specialist_%28PS%29_Ilan_Ramon_%28right%29_during_STS-107.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Commander_(CDR)_Rick_D._Husband_(left)_and_Payload_Specialist_(PS)_Ilan_Ramon_(right)_during_STS-107.jpg)

Commander (CDR) Rick D. Husband (left) and Payload Specialist (PS) Ilan Ramon (right) during STS-107

*   [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107") (January 16 to February 1, 2003) aboard the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") was a 16-day mission during which the crew performed over 80 experiments testing applications of [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microgravity "Microgravity") to gain insight into the environment of space and improve life on Earth as well as enable future space exploration. The mission ended on the morning of February 1 when the shuttle disintegrated upon reentry killing all crew members, including Husband (see [Space Shuttle _Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster")).

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/Rick_Husband%27s_Camaro_on_display_at_Rick_Husband_Amarillo_International_Airport.jpg/250px-Rick_Husband%27s_Camaro_on_display_at_Rick_Husband_Amarillo_International_Airport.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rick_Husband's_Camaro_on_display_at_Rick_Husband_Amarillo_International_Airport.jpg)

Husband's wife, Evelyn (born September 18, 1958), details her [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") life with Rick and his struggles to fulfill his lifelong dream to become an astronaut in the 2004 book _High Calling: The Courageous Life and Faith of Space Shuttle Columbia Commander Rick Husband_ co-written with Donna VanLiere. They had two children together: Laura Marie (born October 5, 1990) and Matthew (born August 3, 1995). Evelyn married Bill Thompson in January 2008 and was the keynote speaker for the memorial ceremony at the Astronaut Memorial "Space Mirror" at the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), five years after the Space Shuttle _Columbia_ tragedy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-7)

**Rick Douglas Husband** (July 12, 1957– February 1, 2003) was an American [astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut") and [fighter pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighter_pilot "Fighter pilot"). He traveled into space twice: as pilot of [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96") and commander of [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"). Husband and the rest of the crew of STS-107 were killed when _Columbia_[disintegrated during reentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") into the [Earth's atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere"). He is also a recipient of the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").

## Early life, education and training

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life, education and training")]

Husband was born on July 12, 1957, in [Amarillo, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amarillo,_Texas "Amarillo, Texas").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-NASA_Bio-1) At age 17, he earned his pilot's license while flying out of [Tradewind Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tradewind_Airport "Tradewind Airport"). Husband graduated with honors from [Amarillo High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amarillo_High_School "Amarillo High School") in 1975.

Husband earned a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [mechanical engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanical_engineering "Mechanical engineering") from [Texas Tech University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Tech_University "Texas Tech University") in 1980 after five years of study. He earned his [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree from [Fresno State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresno_State_University "Fresno State University"). Upon graduation, Husband was commissioned as a pilot in the [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force"), having been enrolled in [ROTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ROTC "ROTC") his last two years of college. Husband underwent pilot training at [Vance Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vance_Air_Force_Base "Vance Air Force Base"), in [Enid, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enid,_Oklahoma "Enid, Oklahoma"). This was followed by Land Survival School at [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base"), in [Spokane, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington"), and [Fighter Lead-in School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trainer_aircraft#Lead-in_fighter_training "Trainer aircraft") in New Mexico. After he got married on February 27, 1982, Husband trained in the [F-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-4 "F-4") at [Homestead Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homestead_Air_Force_Base "Homestead Air Force Base") next.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-Rick-2)

## U.S. Air Force career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: U.S. Air Force career")]

Husband was assigned to a squadron at [Moody Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Air_Force_Base "Moody Air Force Base") in [Valdosta, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valdosta,_Georgia "Valdosta, Georgia"), flying the F-4E. He then transferred to [George AFB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_AFB "George AFB"), in [Victorville, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorville,_California "Victorville, California") in December 1985, where Husband became an F-4 instructor. By then, he had accumulated 1000 hours of flying time.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-Rick-2):30,32

In December 1987, Husband was assigned to [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), where he attended the [USAF Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USAF_Test_Pilot_School "USAF Test Pilot School") class 88A along with future [Canadian Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Space_Agency "Canadian Space Agency") astronaut [Chris Hadfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hadfield "Chris Hadfield"). Upon completion of test pilot school, Husband served as a test pilot flying the F-4 and all five models of the [F-15 Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-15_Eagle "F-15 Eagle"). In the F-15 Combined Test Force, he was the program manager for the [Pratt & Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratt_&_Whitney "Pratt & Whitney")[F100-PW-229](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratt_&_Whitney_F100#F100-PW-229 "Pratt & Whitney F100") increased performance engine and also served as the F-15 Aerial Demonstration Pilot.

In June 1992, Husband was assigned to the Aircraft and Armament Evaluation Establishment at [Boscombe Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boscombe_Down "Boscombe Down"), England, as an exchange test pilot with the [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force"). At Boscombe Down, he was the Tornado GR1 and GR4 Project Pilot and served as a test pilot in the Hawk, Hunter, Buccaneer, Jet Provost, Tucano, and Harvard.

Husband logged over 3,800 hours of flight time in more than 40 different types of [aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft "Aircraft").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-NASA_Bio-1)

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Husband was selected as an astronaut candidate by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") in December 1994, the same week he was promoted to lieutenant colonel.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-Rick-2):67 Husband reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in March 1995 to begin a year of training and evaluation. Upon completion of training, he was named the Astronaut Office representative for Advanced Projects at Johnson Space Center, working on [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") Upgrades, the [Crew Return Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crew_Return_Vehicle "Crew Return Vehicle") (CRV) and studies to return to the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon") and travel to [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"). Husband eventually served as Chief of Safety for the [Astronaut Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_Office "Astronaut Office"). In 1999, he flew as pilot on [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96") and logged 235 hours and 13 minutes in [space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_space "Outer space"). Husband was later assigned to command the crew of [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), which was launched early in 2003. Along with the rest of the STS-107 crew, he was killed upon reentry when the shuttle disintegrated over Texas.

## Shuttle missions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Shuttle missions")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/STS-96_Rick_Husband_and_Tamara_Jernigan.jpg/250px-STS-96_Rick_Husband_and_Tamara_Jernigan.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-96_Rick_Husband_and_Tamara_Jernigan.jpg)

Pilot (PLT) Rick D. Husband (left) and EVA Specialist [Tamara E. Jernigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamara_E._Jernigan "Tamara E. Jernigan") (right) during STS-96

*   [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96") (May 27 to June 6, 1999) aboard the [Space Shuttle _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery") was a 10-day mission during which the crew performed the first docking with the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") and delivered four tons of logistics and supplies in preparation for the arrival of the [first crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_1 "Expedition 1") to live on the station early the following year. The mission was accomplished in 153 Earth orbits, traveling 4 million miles in 9 days, 19 hours and 13 minutes.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Commander_%28CDR%29_Rick_D._Husband_%28left%29_and_Payload_Specialist_%28PS%29_Ilan_Ramon_%28right%29_during_STS-107.jpg/250px-Commander_%28CDR%29_Rick_D._Husband_%28left%29_and_Payload_Specialist_%28PS%29_Ilan_Ramon_%28right%29_during_STS-107.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Commander_(CDR)_Rick_D._Husband_(left)_and_Payload_Specialist_(PS)_Ilan_Ramon_(right)_during_STS-107.jpg)

Commander (CDR) Rick D. Husband (left) and Payload Specialist (PS) Ilan Ramon (right) during STS-107

*   [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107") (January 16 to February 1, 2003) aboard the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") was a 16-day mission during which the crew performed over 80 experiments testing applications of [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microgravity "Microgravity") to gain insight into the environment of space and improve life on Earth as well as enable future space exploration. The mission ended on the morning of February 1 when the shuttle disintegrated upon reentry killing all crew members, including Husband (see [Space Shuttle _Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster")).

*   Rick Husband Boulevard [Howardwick, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howardwick,_Texas "Howardwick, Texas").

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rick_Husband&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/Rick_Husband%27s_Camaro_on_display_at_Rick_Husband_Amarillo_International_Airport.jpg/250px-Rick_Husband%27s_Camaro_on_display_at_Rick_Husband_Amarillo_International_Airport.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rick_Husband's_Camaro_on_display_at_Rick_Husband_Amarillo_International_Airport.jpg)

Husband's Camaro on display at Rick Husband Amarillo International Airport

Husband's wife, Evelyn (born September 18, 1958), details her [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") life with Rick and his struggles to fulfill his lifelong dream to become an astronaut in the 2004 book _High Calling: The Courageous Life and Faith of Space Shuttle Columbia Commander Rick Husband_ co-written with Donna VanLiere. They had two children together: Laura Marie (born October 5, 1990) and Matthew (born August 3, 1995). Evelyn married Bill Thompson in January 2008 and was the keynote speaker for the memorial ceremony at the Astronaut Memorial "Space Mirror" at the [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") in [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), five years after the Space Shuttle _Columbia_ tragedy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Husband#cite_note-7)

**William Cameron "Willie" McCool** ([né](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name "Birth name")**Graham**; September 23, 1961– February 1, 2003) was an American [naval officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") and [aviator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_naval_aviator "United States naval aviator"), [test pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_pilot "Test pilot"), [aeronautical engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_engineer "Aeronautical engineer"), and [NASA astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_astronaut "NASA astronaut"), who was the pilot of [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") mission [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"). He and the rest of the crew of STS-107 were killed when _Columbia_[disintegrated during reentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") into the atmosphere.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NYT-20071205-2) McCool was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_C._McCool&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

McCool was born on September 23, 1961, in [San Diego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego "San Diego"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-5) His parents divorced when McCool was young, and in 1969, his mother married Barent McCool, a Naval aviator.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-usnamh-6) McCool was active in the [Boy Scouts of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_Scouts_of_America "Boy Scouts of America"), where he became an [Eagle Scout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagle_Scout_(Boy_Scouts_of_America) "Eagle Scout (Boy Scouts of America)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-honor-8) McCool attended [John F. Kennedy High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_High_School_(Guam) "John F. Kennedy High School (Guam)") in [Tamuning, Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamuning,_Guam "Tamuning, Guam") from 1967 to 1977.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-9) His family relocated to [Lubbock, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubbock,_Texas "Lubbock, Texas"), where he graduated from [Coronado High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronado_High_School_(Lubbock) "Coronado High School (Lubbock)") in 1979.

McCool then enrolled at the [United States Naval Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Academy "United States Naval Academy"), where he served as team captain of the U.S. Naval Academy [Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") team his senior year. He received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [Applied Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applied_Science "Applied Science") in 1983, graduating second of 1,083 in his class.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NYT-20071205-2) After graduating, he became a member of the U.S. Naval Academy Alumni Association. McCool received a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in [Computer Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_Science "Computer Science") from the [University of Maryland, College Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland,_College_Park "University of Maryland, College Park") in 1985.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1) In 1991, McCool graduated from the [United States Naval Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Test_Pilot_School "United States Naval Test Pilot School"), [Naval Air Station Patuxent River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Air_Station_Patuxent_River "Naval Air Station Patuxent River") in Class 101, and he was presented the "Outstanding Student" and "Best DT-II Thesis" awards as a graduate.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-usnamh-6) In 1992, he received a Master of Science in [Aeronautical Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_Engineering "Aeronautical Engineering") from the U.S. [Naval Postgraduate School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Postgraduate_School "Naval Postgraduate School").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

## Flight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_C._McCool&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Flight experience")]

McCool completed flight training and was designated a [Naval Aviator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Aviator "Naval Aviator") in August 1986. He was assigned to Tactical Electronic Warfare Squadron 129 ([VAQ-129](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VAQ-129 "VAQ-129")) at [NAS Whidbey Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Whidbey_Island "NAS Whidbey Island"), [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state) "Washington (state)"), for initial [EA-6B Prowler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA-6B_Prowler "EA-6B Prowler") training. McCool's first operational tour was with Tactical Electronic Warfare Squadron 133 ([VAQ-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VAQ-133 "VAQ-133")), where he made two deployments aboard the [aircraft carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_carrier "Aircraft carrier")[USS _Coral Sea_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Coral_Sea_(CV-43) "USS Coral Sea (CV-43)") to the [Mediterranean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea") and received designation as a wing-qualified [landing signal officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_signal_officer "Landing signal officer") (LSO). In November 1989, McCool was selected for the U.S. Naval Postgraduate School/[Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Test_Pilot_School "United States Naval Test Pilot School") (TPS) Cooperative Education Program.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

After graduating from TPS in June 1992, McCool worked as a [TA-4J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TA-4J "TA-4J") and EA-6B test pilot in Flight Systems Department of Strike Aircraft Test Directorate at [NAS Patuxent River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Patuxent_River "NAS Patuxent River"), [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"). He was responsible for the management and conduct of a wide variety of projects, ranging from airframe fatigue life studies to numerous avionics upgrades. However, McCool's primary efforts were dedicated to flight test of the [Advanced Capability (ADVCAP) EA-6B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Capability_EA-6B "Advanced Capability EA-6B"). Following his Patuxent River tour, McCool returned to Whidbey Island, and was assigned to Tactical Electronic Warfare Squadron 132 ([VAQ-132](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VAQ-132 "VAQ-132")) aboard the carrier [USS _Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Enterprise_(CVN-65) "USS Enterprise (CVN-65)"). He served as Administrative and Operations Officer with the squadron through their work-up cycle, receiving notice of his NASA selection while embarked on _Enterprise_ for her final pre-deployment at sea period.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

McCool accumulated over 2,800 flight hours in 24 aircraft as well as more than 400 carrier [arrestments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arresting_gear "Arresting gear"), also known as "traps".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-usnamh-6)

## NASA experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_C._McCool&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA experience")]

Selected by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") in April 1996, McCool reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") the following August.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-usnamh-6) He completed two years of training and evaluation, and was qualified for flight assignment as a pilot. Initially assigned to the Computer Support Branch, McCool also served as technical assistant to the director of flight crew operations, and worked Shuttle cockpit upgrade issues for the Astronaut Office.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

### Spaceflight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_C._McCool&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Spaceflight experience")]

Main article: [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")

McCool was pilot of Space Shuttle mission [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), January 16 to February 1, 2003, logging 15 days, 22 hours and 20 minutes in space. The 16-day flight was a dedicated science and research mission. Working 24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments. According to NASA, McCool said of the unique view he and his crewmates had from Columbia:[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-107mem-11)

> From our orbital vantage point, we observe an earth without borders, full of peace, beauty and magnificence, and we pray that humanity as a whole can imagine a borderless world as we see it and strive to live as one in peace.

—William Cameron McCool, 29 January 2003 onboard _Columbia_

STS-107's mission ended abruptly on February 1, 2003, when [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") broke up over the southern United States during re-entry, 16 minutes before scheduled landing. All seven crew members were killed.

McCool was posthumously awarded the [NASA Space Flight Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Space_Flight_Medal "NASA Space Flight Medal"), the [NASA Distinguished Service Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Distinguished_Service_Medal "NASA Distinguished Service Medal"), the [Defense Distinguished Service Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_Distinguished_Service_Medal "Defense Distinguished Service Medal") (DDSM), and the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_C._McCool&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

McCool's favorite song was "[Imagine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagine_(John_Lennon_song) "Imagine (John Lennon song)")" by [John Lennon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lennon "John Lennon"), which was played during the STS-107 mission. His favorite band was [Radiohead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiohead "Radiohead"), and the song "[Fake Plastic Trees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fake_Plastic_Trees "Fake Plastic Trees")" was played by [Mission Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Control "Mission Control") as a wake-up call.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-12)

McCool was survived by his wife, Lani, and their three sons. He is buried in [Anacortes, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anacortes,_Washington "Anacortes, Washington"), where he lived at the time of his death.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NYT-20071205-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-13)

**William Cameron "Willie" McCool** ([né](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name "Birth name")**Graham**; September 23, 1961– February 1, 2003) was an American [naval officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") and [aviator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_naval_aviator "United States naval aviator"), [test pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_pilot "Test pilot"), [aeronautical engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_engineer "Aeronautical engineer"), and [NASA astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_astronaut "NASA astronaut"), who was the pilot of [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") mission [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"). He and the rest of the crew of STS-107 were killed when _Columbia_[disintegrated during reentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") into the atmosphere.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NYT-20071205-2) McCool was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_C._McCool&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

McCool was born on September 23, 1961, in [San Diego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego "San Diego"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-5) His parents divorced when McCool was young, and in 1969, his mother married Barent McCool, a Naval aviator.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-usnamh-6) McCool was active in the [Boy Scouts of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_Scouts_of_America "Boy Scouts of America"), where he became an [Eagle Scout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagle_Scout_(Boy_Scouts_of_America) "Eagle Scout (Boy Scouts of America)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-honor-8) McCool attended [John F. Kennedy High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_High_School_(Guam) "John F. Kennedy High School (Guam)") in [Tamuning, Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamuning,_Guam "Tamuning, Guam") from 1967 to 1977.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-9) His family relocated to [Lubbock, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubbock,_Texas "Lubbock, Texas"), where he graduated from [Coronado High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronado_High_School_(Lubbock) "Coronado High School (Lubbock)") in 1979.

McCool then enrolled at the [United States Naval Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Academy "United States Naval Academy"), where he served as team captain of the U.S. Naval Academy [Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") team his senior year. He received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [Applied Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applied_Science "Applied Science") in 1983, graduating second of 1,083 in his class.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NYT-20071205-2) After graduating, he became a member of the U.S. Naval Academy Alumni Association. McCool received a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in [Computer Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_Science "Computer Science") from the [University of Maryland, College Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland,_College_Park "University of Maryland, College Park") in 1985.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1) In 1991, McCool graduated from the [United States Naval Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Test_Pilot_School "United States Naval Test Pilot School"), [Naval Air Station Patuxent River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Air_Station_Patuxent_River "Naval Air Station Patuxent River") in Class 101, and he was presented the "Outstanding Student" and "Best DT-II Thesis" awards as a graduate.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-usnamh-6) In 1992, he received a Master of Science in [Aeronautical Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_Engineering "Aeronautical Engineering") from the U.S. [Naval Postgraduate School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Postgraduate_School "Naval Postgraduate School").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

## Flight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_C._McCool&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Flight experience")]

McCool completed flight training and was designated a [Naval Aviator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Aviator "Naval Aviator") in August 1986. He was assigned to Tactical Electronic Warfare Squadron 129 ([VAQ-129](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VAQ-129 "VAQ-129")) at [NAS Whidbey Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Whidbey_Island "NAS Whidbey Island"), [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state) "Washington (state)"), for initial [EA-6B Prowler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA-6B_Prowler "EA-6B Prowler") training. McCool's first operational tour was with Tactical Electronic Warfare Squadron 133 ([VAQ-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VAQ-133 "VAQ-133")), where he made two deployments aboard the [aircraft carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_carrier "Aircraft carrier")[USS _Coral Sea_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Coral_Sea_(CV-43) "USS Coral Sea (CV-43)") to the [Mediterranean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea") and received designation as a wing-qualified [landing signal officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_signal_officer "Landing signal officer") (LSO). In November 1989, McCool was selected for the U.S. Naval Postgraduate School/[Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Naval_Test_Pilot_School "United States Naval Test Pilot School") (TPS) Cooperative Education Program.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

After graduating from TPS in June 1992, McCool worked as a [TA-4J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TA-4J "TA-4J") and EA-6B test pilot in Flight Systems Department of Strike Aircraft Test Directorate at [NAS Patuxent River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Patuxent_River "NAS Patuxent River"), [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"). He was responsible for the management and conduct of a wide variety of projects, ranging from airframe fatigue life studies to numerous avionics upgrades. However, McCool's primary efforts were dedicated to flight test of the [Advanced Capability (ADVCAP) EA-6B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Capability_EA-6B "Advanced Capability EA-6B"). Following his Patuxent River tour, McCool returned to Whidbey Island, and was assigned to Tactical Electronic Warfare Squadron 132 ([VAQ-132](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VAQ-132 "VAQ-132")) aboard the carrier [USS _Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Enterprise_(CVN-65) "USS Enterprise (CVN-65)"). He served as Administrative and Operations Officer with the squadron through their work-up cycle, receiving notice of his NASA selection while embarked on _Enterprise_ for her final pre-deployment at sea period.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

McCool accumulated over 2,800 flight hours in 24 aircraft as well as more than 400 carrier [arrestments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arresting_gear "Arresting gear"), also known as "traps".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-usnamh-6)

## NASA experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_C._McCool&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA experience")]

Selected by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") in April 1996, McCool reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") the following August.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-usnamh-6) He completed two years of training and evaluation, and was qualified for flight assignment as a pilot. Initially assigned to the Computer Support Branch, McCool also served as technical assistant to the director of flight crew operations, and worked Shuttle cockpit upgrade issues for the Astronaut Office.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

### Spaceflight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_C._McCool&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Spaceflight experience")]

Main article: [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")

McCool was pilot of Space Shuttle mission [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), January 16 to February 1, 2003, logging 15 days, 22 hours and 20 minutes in space. The 16-day flight was a dedicated science and research mission. Working 24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments. According to NASA, McCool said of the unique view he and his crewmates had from Columbia:[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-107mem-11)

> From our orbital vantage point, we observe an earth without borders, full of peace, beauty and magnificence, and we pray that humanity as a whole can imagine a borderless world as we see it and strive to live as one in peace.

—William Cameron McCool, 29 January 2003 onboard _Columbia_

STS-107's mission ended abruptly on February 1, 2003, when [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") broke up over the southern United States during re-entry, 16 minutes before scheduled landing. All seven crew members were killed.

McCool was posthumously awarded the [NASA Space Flight Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Space_Flight_Medal "NASA Space Flight Medal"), the [NASA Distinguished Service Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Distinguished_Service_Medal "NASA Distinguished Service Medal"), the [Defense Distinguished Service Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_Distinguished_Service_Medal "Defense Distinguished Service Medal") (DDSM), and the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NASA-JSC-1)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=William_C._McCool&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

McCool's favorite song was "[Imagine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagine_(John_Lennon_song) "Imagine (John Lennon song)")" by [John Lennon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lennon "John Lennon"), which was played during the STS-107 mission. His favorite band was [Radiohead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiohead "Radiohead"), and the song "[Fake Plastic Trees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fake_Plastic_Trees "Fake Plastic Trees")" was played by [Mission Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Control "Mission Control") as a wake-up call.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-12)

McCool was survived by his wife, Lani, and their three sons. He is buried in [Anacortes, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anacortes,_Washington "Anacortes, Washington"), where he lived at the time of his death.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-NYT-20071205-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_C._McCool#cite_note-13)

**David McDowell Brown** (April 16, 1956 – February 1, 2003) was a [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy")[captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(United_States_O-6) "Captain (United States O-6)") and [NASA astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_astronaut "NASA astronaut"). He died on his first [spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceflight "Spaceflight"), when the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") ([STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")) disintegrated during orbital reentry into the Earth's atmosphere. Brown became an astronaut in 1996 but had not served on a space mission prior to the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"). He was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-1)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Brown was born on April 16, 1956, in [Arlington, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Virginia "Arlington, Virginia"). As a youth, he attended McKinley Elementary School and Swanson Middle School, and graduated from [Yorktown High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorktown_High_School_(Virginia) "Yorktown High School (Virginia)") in Arlington in 1974. Brown was a member of the [Boy Scouts of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_Scouts_of_America "Boy Scouts of America") and achieved its second-highest rank, [Life Scout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_Scout "Life Scout"). [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-:0-2) He received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology "Biology") from the [College of William & Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_William_&_Mary "College of William & Mary") in 1978, and a [Doctor of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine "Doctor of Medicine") from the [Eastern Virginia Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Virginia_Medical_School "Eastern Virginia Medical School") in 1982.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-:0-2)

## Military career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career")]

Brown joined the [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Navy "U.S. Navy") after his internship at the [Medical University of South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_University_of_South_Carolina "Medical University of South Carolina"). Upon completion of [flight surgeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_surgeon "Flight surgeon") training in 1984, Brown reported to the Navy Branch Hospital in [Adak, Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adak,_Alaska "Adak, Alaska"), as Director of Medical Services.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-3) He was then assigned to [Carrier Air Wing Fifteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrier_Air_Wing_Fifteen "Carrier Air Wing Fifteen") which deployed aboard the [aircraft carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_carrier "Aircraft carrier")[USS _Carl Vinson_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Carl_Vinson "USS Carl Vinson") in the Western Pacific. In 1988, Brown became the only flight surgeon in a 10-year period to be chosen for pilot training. He was ultimately designated a [Naval Aviator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Aviator "Naval Aviator") in 1990 at [NAS Chase Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Chase_Field "NAS Chase Field") in [Beeville, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beeville,_Texas "Beeville, Texas"), ranking number one in his class. Brown was then sent for training and carrier qualification in the [A-6E Intruder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-6_Intruder "A-6 Intruder"). In 1991, he reported to the Naval Strike Warfare Center at [NAS Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Fallon "NAS Fallon"), [Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada "Nevada"), serving as a Strike Leader Attack Training Syllabus Instructor and a Contingency Cell Planning Officer. Brown was also qualified in the [F/A-18 Hornet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F/A-18_Hornet "F/A-18 Hornet") and deployed from Japan in 1992 aboard [USS _Independence_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Independence_(CV-62) "USS Independence (CV-62)") flying the A-6E with [VA-115](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VFA-115 "VFA-115"). In 1995, he reported to the [U.S. Naval Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Test_Pilot_School "U.S. Naval Test Pilot School") at [NAS Patuxent River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Patuxent_River "NAS Patuxent River"), Maryland as their flight surgeon, where Brown also flew the [T-38 Talon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-38_Talon "T-38 Talon").

Brown logged over 2,700 flight hours, with 1,700 in high-performance military aircraft. He was qualified as the first pilot in NASA T-38 aircraft and held a [Federal Communications Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission "Federal Communications Commission") (FCC) issued Technician Class [amateur radio license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_radio_license "Amateur radio license") with the [call sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_sign "Call sign") KC5ZTC.

Brown also served as President of the International Association of Military Flight Surgeon Pilots, an associate fellow at the [Aerospace Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_Medical_Association "Aerospace Medical Association"), and a member of the Society of U.S. Naval Flight Surgeons.

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Selected by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") in April 1996, Brown reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1996. He completed two years of training and evaluation and was qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist. Brown was initially assigned to support payload development for the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"), followed by the astronaut support team responsible for orbiter cockpit setup, crew strap-in, and landing recovery.

On April 21, 2001, Brown appeared on [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN") as an expert on [g-force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G-force "G-force") loading on the human body that led to the cancellation of the [Firestone Firehawk 600](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firestone_Firehawk_600 "Firestone Firehawk 600")[CART](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Championship_Auto_Racing_Teams "Championship Auto Racing Teams") race.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-4)

Brown flew aboard [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") on [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), logging 15 days, 22 hours, and 20 minutes in space from January 16 to February 1, 2003. The flight was a dedicated science and research mission. Working 24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments. On February 1, 2003, all seven members of _Columbia'_ s crew perished during reentry, 16 minutes before the scheduled landing.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/US_Navy_030312-N-2147L-001_U.S._Navy_Capt._David_M._Brown%2C_NASA_Astronaut_laid_to_rest.jpg/250px-US_Navy_030312-N-2147L-001_U.S._Navy_Capt._David_M._Brown%2C_NASA_Astronaut_laid_to_rest.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Navy_030312-N-2147L-001_U.S._Navy_Capt._David_M._Brown,_NASA_Astronaut_laid_to_rest.jpg)

Brown's funeral services at [Arlington National Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery "Arlington National Cemetery") on March 12, 2003

The only unmarried member of the STS-107 crew, Brown had previously been romantically involved with NASA engineer Ann Micklos. The couple ended their relationship shortly before the mission and remained close friends until his death.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-5) The crew of STS-107 had formed a close friendship during their training, and Brown had been preparing a video to commemorate this once they returned from the mission. He is buried in [Arlington National Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery "Arlington National Cemetery").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-7)

*   Lunar crater D. Brown is named after Brown.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-8)
*   Brown Hall, in the Columbia Village apartments, at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology") is named after him.
*   He is the first person to be posthumously awarded the William & Mary Alumni Association's Alumni Medal.
*   The Laurel B. Clark and David M. Brown Aerospace Medicine Academic Center, located at the Naval Aerospace Medical Institute, is named after him.
*   The Captain David Brown Aerospace and Medical Research Endowment was established in his memory to help deserving students attending Eastern Virginia Medical School.
*   The planetarium of [Arlington Public Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_Public_Schools "Arlington Public Schools"), from which Brown graduated, was renamed the [David M. Brown Planetarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_Public_Schools#Special_facilities "Arlington Public Schools").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-:0-2)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-9)
*   The Dave Brown Memorial Park in [Friendswood, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendswood,_Texas "Friendswood, Texas"), is named after him.
*   The annual Astronaut Dave Brown Memorial gymnastics meet is held at the [College of William & Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_William_&_Mary "College of William & Mary") in his honor, where Dave Brown was a gymnast.
*   Yorktown High School Crew Team Men's Varsity 8 boat name Captain David M. Brown - c. 2003
*   Circle Oil Hill Elementary of [Circle USD 375](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_USD_375 "Circle USD 375") in Kansas grants a scholarship each year - David Brown Hopes & Dreams Scholarship. This scholarship was first awarded in 2005.

**David McDowell Brown** (April 16, 1956 – February 1, 2003) was a [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy")[captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(United_States_O-6) "Captain (United States O-6)") and [NASA astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_astronaut "NASA astronaut"). He died on his first [spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceflight "Spaceflight"), when the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") ([STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")) disintegrated during orbital reentry into the Earth's atmosphere. Brown became an astronaut in 1996 but had not served on a space mission prior to the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"). He was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-1)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Brown was born on April 16, 1956, in [Arlington, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington,_Virginia "Arlington, Virginia"). As a youth, he attended McKinley Elementary School and Swanson Middle School, and graduated from [Yorktown High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorktown_High_School_(Virginia) "Yorktown High School (Virginia)") in Arlington in 1974. Brown was a member of the [Boy Scouts of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boy_Scouts_of_America "Boy Scouts of America") and achieved its second-highest rank, [Life Scout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_Scout "Life Scout"). [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-:0-2) He received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology "Biology") from the [College of William & Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_William_&_Mary "College of William & Mary") in 1978, and a [Doctor of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine "Doctor of Medicine") from the [Eastern Virginia Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Virginia_Medical_School "Eastern Virginia Medical School") in 1982.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-:0-2)

## Military career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career")]

Brown joined the [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Navy "U.S. Navy") after his internship at the [Medical University of South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_University_of_South_Carolina "Medical University of South Carolina"). Upon completion of [flight surgeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_surgeon "Flight surgeon") training in 1984, Brown reported to the Navy Branch Hospital in [Adak, Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adak,_Alaska "Adak, Alaska"), as Director of Medical Services.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-3) He was then assigned to [Carrier Air Wing Fifteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrier_Air_Wing_Fifteen "Carrier Air Wing Fifteen") which deployed aboard the [aircraft carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_carrier "Aircraft carrier")[USS _Carl Vinson_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Carl_Vinson "USS Carl Vinson") in the Western Pacific. In 1988, Brown became the only flight surgeon in a 10-year period to be chosen for pilot training. He was ultimately designated a [Naval Aviator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Aviator "Naval Aviator") in 1990 at [NAS Chase Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Chase_Field "NAS Chase Field") in [Beeville, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beeville,_Texas "Beeville, Texas"), ranking number one in his class. Brown was then sent for training and carrier qualification in the [A-6E Intruder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-6_Intruder "A-6 Intruder"). In 1991, he reported to the Naval Strike Warfare Center at [NAS Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Fallon "NAS Fallon"), [Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada "Nevada"), serving as a Strike Leader Attack Training Syllabus Instructor and a Contingency Cell Planning Officer. Brown was also qualified in the [F/A-18 Hornet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F/A-18_Hornet "F/A-18 Hornet") and deployed from Japan in 1992 aboard [USS _Independence_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Independence_(CV-62) "USS Independence (CV-62)") flying the A-6E with [VA-115](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VFA-115 "VFA-115"). In 1995, he reported to the [U.S. Naval Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Test_Pilot_School "U.S. Naval Test Pilot School") at [NAS Patuxent River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Patuxent_River "NAS Patuxent River"), Maryland as their flight surgeon, where Brown also flew the [T-38 Talon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-38_Talon "T-38 Talon").

Brown logged over 2,700 flight hours, with 1,700 in high-performance military aircraft. He was qualified as the first pilot in NASA T-38 aircraft and held a [Federal Communications Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission "Federal Communications Commission") (FCC) issued Technician Class [amateur radio license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_radio_license "Amateur radio license") with the [call sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_sign "Call sign") KC5ZTC.

Brown also served as President of the International Association of Military Flight Surgeon Pilots, an associate fellow at the [Aerospace Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_Medical_Association "Aerospace Medical Association"), and a member of the Society of U.S. Naval Flight Surgeons.

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Selected by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") in April 1996, Brown reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1996. He completed two years of training and evaluation and was qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist. Brown was initially assigned to support payload development for the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"), followed by the astronaut support team responsible for orbiter cockpit setup, crew strap-in, and landing recovery.

On April 21, 2001, Brown appeared on [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN") as an expert on [g-force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G-force "G-force") loading on the human body that led to the cancellation of the [Firestone Firehawk 600](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firestone_Firehawk_600 "Firestone Firehawk 600")[CART](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Championship_Auto_Racing_Teams "Championship Auto Racing Teams") race.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-4)

Brown flew aboard [Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") on [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), logging 15 days, 22 hours, and 20 minutes in space from January 16 to February 1, 2003. The flight was a dedicated science and research mission. Working 24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments. On February 1, 2003, all seven members of _Columbia'_ s crew perished during reentry, 16 minutes before the scheduled landing.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/US_Navy_030312-N-2147L-001_U.S._Navy_Capt._David_M._Brown%2C_NASA_Astronaut_laid_to_rest.jpg/250px-US_Navy_030312-N-2147L-001_U.S._Navy_Capt._David_M._Brown%2C_NASA_Astronaut_laid_to_rest.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Navy_030312-N-2147L-001_U.S._Navy_Capt._David_M._Brown,_NASA_Astronaut_laid_to_rest.jpg)

Brown's funeral services at [Arlington National Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery "Arlington National Cemetery") on March 12, 2003

The only unmarried member of the STS-107 crew, Brown had previously been romantically involved with NASA engineer Ann Micklos. The couple ended their relationship shortly before the mission and remained close friends until his death.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-5) The crew of STS-107 had formed a close friendship during their training, and Brown had been preparing a video to commemorate this once they returned from the mission. He is buried in [Arlington National Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery "Arlington National Cemetery").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-7)

## Tributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_M._Brown&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Tributes")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/David_M._Brown_Planetarium%2C_Arlington%2C_Virginia_.jpg/250px-David_M._Brown_Planetarium%2C_Arlington%2C_Virginia_.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:David_M._Brown_Planetarium,_Arlington,_Virginia_.jpg)

The David M. Brown Planetarium in Arlington County, Virginia

*   Asteroid [51825 Davidbrown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51825_Davidbrown "51825 Davidbrown") was named in honor of Brown.
*   Lunar crater D. Brown is named after Brown.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-8)
*   Brown Hall, in the Columbia Village apartments, at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology") is named after him.
*   He is the first person to be posthumously awarded the William & Mary Alumni Association's Alumni Medal.
*   The Laurel B. Clark and David M. Brown Aerospace Medicine Academic Center, located at the Naval Aerospace Medical Institute, is named after him.
*   The Captain David Brown Aerospace and Medical Research Endowment was established in his memory to help deserving students attending Eastern Virginia Medical School.
*   The planetarium of [Arlington Public Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_Public_Schools "Arlington Public Schools"), from which Brown graduated, was renamed the [David M. Brown Planetarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_Public_Schools#Special_facilities "Arlington Public Schools").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-:0-2)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Brown#cite_note-9)
*   The Dave Brown Memorial Park in [Friendswood, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendswood,_Texas "Friendswood, Texas"), is named after him.
*   The annual Astronaut Dave Brown Memorial gymnastics meet is held at the [College of William & Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_William_&_Mary "College of William & Mary") in his honor, where Dave Brown was a gymnast.
*   Yorktown High School Crew Team Men's Varsity 8 boat name Captain David M. Brown - c. 2003
*   Circle Oil Hill Elementary of [Circle USD 375](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_USD_375 "Circle USD 375") in Kansas grants a scholarship each year - David Brown Hopes & Dreams Scholarship. This scholarship was first awarded in 2005.
