## NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: NASA")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Michael_P._Anderson.jpg/250px-Michael_P._Anderson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Michael_P._Anderson.jpg)

Anderson in 1995

Anderson reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in March 1995.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) He completed a year of training and evaluation, and was qualified for flight crew assignment as a [mission specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Specialist "Mission Specialist").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Anderson was initially assigned technical duties in the Flight Support Branch of the [Astronaut Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Astronaut_Corps "NASA Astronaut Corps"), but went on to log more than 593 hours in space aboard two Space Shuttle missions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

### Space Shuttle missions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Space Shuttle missions")]

#### _Endeavour_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Endeavour")]

Main article: [Space Shuttle Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")

Anderson was a mission specialist on [STS-89](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-89 "STS-89")_[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ (January 22–31, 1998), the eighth Shuttle-to-[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir")[Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station") docking mission, during which the crew delivered over 9,000 pounds of scientific equipment, logistical hardware, and water.

In the fifth and last exchange of a U.S. astronaut, STS-89 delivered [Andy Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Thomas "Andy Thomas") to Mir and returned with [David Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wolf_(astronaut) "David Wolf (astronaut)"). The mission's duration was 8 days, 19 hours, and 47 seconds, traveling 3.6 million miles in 138 [orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbits "Orbits") of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:1-3)

#### _Columbia_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Columbia")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Anderson_on_STS-107.jpg/250px-Anderson_on_STS-107.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anderson_on_STS-107.jpg)

Anderson during the STS-107 mission

Main article: [Space Shuttle Columbia disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster")

[STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")[Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") (January 16–February 1, 2003). Anderson served as [payload commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Specialist "Payload Specialist") and lieutenant colonel in charge of science experiments on the _Columbia_, NASA's oldest shuttle.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-6) On February 1, 2003, the shuttle was returning to Earth after a successful 16-day trip to orbit, where the crew had conducted more than 80 scientific experiments.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-7)

Unbeknownst to her crew, the orbiter had suffered critical damage during its launch on January 16, when foam from the fuel tank's insulation fell off and tore a hole in _Columbia's_ left wing.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:2-8) During re-entry, the hole allowed super-hot [atmospheric gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Earth "Atmosphere of Earth") to penetrate the orbiter's wing, leading to its destruction.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:2-8) The mission's duration was 15 days, 22 hours, and 20 minutes.

Along with the rest of the STS-107 crew, Anderson was killed upon reentry when the shuttle disintegrated over Texas.

The [_Columbia_ Accident Investigation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") reported[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-9) that, in addition to the _Columbia_'s physical damage, NASA's management culture was partly responsible for the disaster.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-10)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Anderson had a wife, Sandra Hawkins, and two daughters, Kaycee and Sydney. He also had three sisters.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-11)

Anderson and his family lived in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston") at the time of his death, where they attended Grace Community Church.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:3-12) Anderson sang tenor in the church's choir.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:3-12)

*   [Asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid")[51824 Mikeanderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51824_Mikeanderson "51824 Mikeanderson") was posthumously named after Anderson.
*   Anderson Hall, in the Columbia Village apartments at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology") is named after him.
*   Anderson Plaza, the green space in front of the Hixson-Lied Science Center at [Creighton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_University "Creighton University") was named after him in a compromise between the student body, who wanted the Science Center named for Anderson, and the administration who had already sold the naming rights to the Hixson-Lied family.
*   Blair Elementary School on [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base") in Washington was renamed Michael Anderson Elementary School in January 2004. Anderson attended the school as a fifth-grader.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-13)
*   Avondale Elementary School in [Avondale, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avondale,_Arizona "Avondale, Arizona") was renamed Michael Anderson Elementary in his honor. Anderson attended school there when he was in the third grade, and one of the school T-shirts was aboard the _Columbia_ on its last voyage.
*   In 2003, Anderson was inducted into the International Forest of Friendship, in Atchison, KS as part of a memorial to the _Columbia_ astronauts.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-14)
*   Anderson Park in [Canton, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Mississippi "Canton, Mississippi") was dedicated in June 2004.
*   An outdoor bronze statue of Anderson was unveiled in [Spokane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington") in June 2005. Larger-than-life, it was created by local artist Dorothy Fowler, and shows Anderson kneeling with his helmet in one hand and a dove in the other.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-16)
*   A duplicate statue was dedicated at the [Museum of Flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Flight "Museum of Flight") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle") in June 2009[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-17) and the museum launched an aerospace program in his honor.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-18)
*   An outdoor mural in the city of Plattsburgh was unveiled in October 2020 honoring Anderson. On July 4, 2021, the city of Plattsburgh held a dedication for the mural, where the Anderson family was given a key to the city and led the annual Independence Day parade.
*   Lunar crater M. Anderson is named after Anderson.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-19)
*   The Creighton University Physics Department, from which Anderson received his master's degree, maintains a statue and physics scholarship in his honor.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-21)

**Michael Phillip Anderson** (December 25, 1959 – February 1, 2003) was a [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") officer and [NASA astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_astronaut "NASA astronaut"). He and his six fellow crew members were killed in the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") when the [craft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")[disintegrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-flight_breakup "In-flight breakup") during its [re-entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reentry_(orbital) "Reentry (orbital)") into the [Earth's atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:4-1) Anderson served as the payload commander and lieutenant colonel in charge of science experiments on the _Columbia_. He was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Michael Philip Anderson was born in [Plattsburgh, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh,_New_York "Plattsburgh, New York") on December 25, 1959, to Barbara and Bobbie Anderson. He was their third child and only son. Bobbie serviced jets at [Plattsburgh Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh_Air_Force_Base "Plattsburgh Air Force Base") in Plattsburgh[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) and was transferred to [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base"), about 12 miles (19 km) away from [Spokane, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington"), which Anderson spoke of as his hometown.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:1-3) Anderson graduated from [Cheney High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney_School_District "Cheney School District") in [Cheney, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney,_Washington "Cheney, Washington"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-4) one of four [African Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") in a class of 200 students.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

In 1981, Anderson graduated with a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics "Physics") and [astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomy "Astronomy") from the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle"). In 1990, he earned a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in physics from [Creighton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_University "Creighton University") in [Omaha, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaha,_Nebraska "Omaha, Nebraska").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-5)

## Air Force career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Air Force career")]

Upon Anderson's graduation from the University of Washington, he was commissioned a [second lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Lieutenant "Second Lieutenant") in the [U.S. Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Air_Force "U.S. Air Force").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) After completing a year of technical training at [Keesler Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keesler_Air_Force_Base "Keesler Air Force Base") in [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), Anderson was assigned to [Randolph Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph_Air_Force_Base "Randolph Air Force Base") in [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) At Randolph, he served as chief of communication maintenance for the 2015th Communication Squadron and later as director of information system maintenance for the 1920th Information System Group.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

In 1986, Anderson was selected to attend [Undergraduate Pilot Training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate_Pilot_Training "Undergraduate Pilot Training") at [Vance Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vance_Air_Force_Base "Vance Air Force Base"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Upon graduation, he was assigned to the [2d Airborne Command and Control Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2d_Airborne_Command_and_Control_Squadron "2d Airborne Command and Control Squadron"), [Offutt Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offutt_Air_Force_Base "Offutt Air Force Base"), [Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska") as an [EC-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_EC-135 "Boeing EC-135") pilot, flying the [Strategic Air Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Air_Command "Strategic Air Command")'s airborne command post code-named "[Looking Glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Looking_Glass "Operation Looking Glass")." Anderson completed his master's degree while stationed at Offutt.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

From January 1991 to September 1992, Anderson served as an aircraft commander and [instructor pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_instructor "Flight instructor") in the [920th Air Refueling Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/920th_Air_Refueling_Squadron "920th Air Refueling Squadron"), [Wurtsmith Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wurtsmith_Air_Force_Base "Wurtsmith Air Force Base"), [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

From September 1992 to February 1995, Anderson was assigned as an instructor pilot and tactics officer in the [380th Air Refueling Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/380th_Air_Refueling_Wing "380th Air Refueling Wing"), [Plattsburgh Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plattsburgh_Air_Force_Base "Plattsburgh Air Force Base"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

Anderson logged more than 3,000 hours of flight time when NASA selected him for astronaut training in December 1994.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Anderson was one of 19 candidates selected from a pool of 2,962 applicants.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

## NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: NASA")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Michael_P._Anderson.jpg/250px-Michael_P._Anderson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Michael_P._Anderson.jpg)

Anderson in 1995

Anderson reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in March 1995.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) He completed a year of training and evaluation, and was qualified for flight crew assignment as a [mission specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Specialist "Mission Specialist").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2) Anderson was initially assigned technical duties in the Flight Support Branch of the [Astronaut Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Astronaut_Corps "NASA Astronaut Corps"), but went on to log more than 593 hours in space aboard two Space Shuttle missions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:0-2)

### Space Shuttle missions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Space Shuttle missions")]

#### _Endeavour_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Endeavour")]

Main article: [Space Shuttle Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")

Anderson was a mission specialist on [STS-89](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-89 "STS-89")_[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ (January 22–31, 1998), the eighth Shuttle-to-[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir")[Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station") docking mission, during which the crew delivered over 9,000 pounds of scientific equipment, logistical hardware, and water.

In the fifth and last exchange of a U.S. astronaut, STS-89 delivered [Andy Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Thomas "Andy Thomas") to Mir and returned with [David Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wolf_(astronaut) "David Wolf (astronaut)"). The mission's duration was 8 days, 19 hours, and 47 seconds, traveling 3.6 million miles in 138 [orbits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbits "Orbits") of the [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:1-3)

#### _Columbia_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Columbia")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Anderson_on_STS-107.jpg/250px-Anderson_on_STS-107.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anderson_on_STS-107.jpg)

Anderson during the STS-107 mission

Main article: [Space Shuttle Columbia disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster")

[STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")[Space Shuttle _Columbia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia") (January 16–February 1, 2003). Anderson served as [payload commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Specialist "Payload Specialist") and lieutenant colonel in charge of science experiments on the _Columbia_, NASA's oldest shuttle.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-6) On February 1, 2003, the shuttle was returning to Earth after a successful 16-day trip to orbit, where the crew had conducted more than 80 scientific experiments.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-7)

Unbeknownst to her crew, the orbiter had suffered critical damage during its launch on January 16, when foam from the fuel tank's insulation fell off and tore a hole in _Columbia's_ left wing.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:2-8) During re-entry, the hole allowed super-hot [atmospheric gases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Earth "Atmosphere of Earth") to penetrate the orbiter's wing, leading to its destruction.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:2-8) The mission's duration was 15 days, 22 hours, and 20 minutes.

Along with the rest of the STS-107 crew, Anderson was killed upon reentry when the shuttle disintegrated over Texas.

The [_Columbia_ Accident Investigation Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Accident_Investigation_Board "Columbia Accident Investigation Board") reported[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-9) that, in addition to the _Columbia_'s physical damage, NASA's management culture was partly responsible for the disaster.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-10)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Anderson had a wife, Sandra Hawkins, and two daughters, Kaycee and Sydney. He also had three sisters.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-11)

Anderson and his family lived in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston") at the time of his death, where they attended Grace Community Church.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:3-12) Anderson sang tenor in the church's choir.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-:3-12)

## Legacy and tributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Michael_P._Anderson&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Legacy and tributes")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/MPAndersonMemHwySign.jpg/250px-MPAndersonMemHwySign.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MPAndersonMemHwySign.jpg)

 Sign along [Washington State Route 904](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_Route_904 "Washington State Route 904"), commemorating  
Lt. Col. Michael P. Anderson.

*   [State Route 904](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_Route_904 "Washington State Route 904"), running through [Cheney, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheney,_Washington "Cheney, Washington"), where Anderson graduated from high school, was renamed in his memory.
*   The science and math wing of Cheney High School is dedicated to his memory.
*   [Asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid")[51824 Mikeanderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51824_Mikeanderson "51824 Mikeanderson") was posthumously named after Anderson.
*   Anderson Hall, in the Columbia Village apartments at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology") is named after him.
*   Anderson Plaza, the green space in front of the Hixson-Lied Science Center at [Creighton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creighton_University "Creighton University") was named after him in a compromise between the student body, who wanted the Science Center named for Anderson, and the administration who had already sold the naming rights to the Hixson-Lied family.
*   Blair Elementary School on [Fairchild Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairchild_Air_Force_Base "Fairchild Air Force Base") in Washington was renamed Michael Anderson Elementary School in January 2004. Anderson attended the school as a fifth-grader.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-13)
*   Avondale Elementary School in [Avondale, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avondale,_Arizona "Avondale, Arizona") was renamed Michael Anderson Elementary in his honor. Anderson attended school there when he was in the third grade, and one of the school T-shirts was aboard the _Columbia_ on its last voyage.
*   In 2003, Anderson was inducted into the International Forest of Friendship, in Atchison, KS as part of a memorial to the _Columbia_ astronauts.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-14)
*   Anderson Park in [Canton, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Mississippi "Canton, Mississippi") was dedicated in June 2004.
*   An outdoor bronze statue of Anderson was unveiled in [Spokane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane,_Washington "Spokane, Washington") in June 2005. Larger-than-life, it was created by local artist Dorothy Fowler, and shows Anderson kneeling with his helmet in one hand and a dove in the other.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-16)
*   A duplicate statue was dedicated at the [Museum of Flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Flight "Museum of Flight") in [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle") in June 2009[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-17) and the museum launched an aerospace program in his honor.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-18)
*   An outdoor mural in the city of Plattsburgh was unveiled in October 2020 honoring Anderson. On July 4, 2021, the city of Plattsburgh held a dedication for the mural, where the Anderson family was given a key to the city and led the annual Independence Day parade.
*   Lunar crater M. Anderson is named after Anderson.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-19)
*   The Creighton University Physics Department, from which Anderson received his master's degree, maintains a statue and physics scholarship in his honor.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_P._Anderson#cite_note-21)

**Ilan Ramon** ([Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language"): אילן רמון; pronounced[[(ʔ)iˈlan ʁaˈmon]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Hebrew "Help:IPA/Hebrew"); June 20, 1954 – February 1, 2003)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-Stone20032-1) was an [Israeli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel")[fighter pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighter_pilot "Fighter pilot") and later the first Israeli [astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). He served as a [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") payload specialist on [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), the fatal mission of _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_, in which he and the six other crew members were killed when the spacecraft [disintegrated during re-entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"). At 48, Ramon was the oldest member of the crew. He is the first foreign recipient of the United States [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor"), which was awarded posthumously.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-2)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Born as Ilan Wolfferman in [Ramat Gan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramat_Gan "Ramat Gan"), Israel, to Tonya (1929–2003) and Eliezer Wolfferman (1923–2006), a family of [Ashkenazi Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashkenazi_Jewish "Ashkenazi Jewish") descent, Ramon grew up in [Beersheba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beersheba "Beersheba"). His father was from [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Jews "German Jews"), and his family fled [Nazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") persecution in 1935. His mother and grandmother were from [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Jews "Polish Jews"), and were [Holocaust survivors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_survivors "Holocaust survivors"), having been in [Auschwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auschwitz "Auschwitz"). They [emigrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aliyah "Aliyah") to Israel in 1949.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-3) Ramon's first name, Ilan, means "tree" in [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-4) Ramon [Hebraizied his surname](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebraization_of_surnames "Hebraization of surnames") from **Wolfferman** to **Ramon**, a more "Israeli ([Sabra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabra_(person) "Sabra (person)"))" name, when he joined the [Israeli Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Air_Force "Israeli Air Force") (IAF). This was customary and expected of IAF pilots, as well as among [IDF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Defense_Forces "Israel Defense Forces") senior officers at the time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-5)

Ramon graduated from high school in 1972. In 1987, he graduated with a [B.Sc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in electronics and computer engineering from [Tel Aviv University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Aviv_University "Tel Aviv University").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-nasabio-6)

## Air Force career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Air Force career")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Colonel_ilan_ramon_%2C_israeli_air_force_website.jpg/250px-Colonel_ilan_ramon_%2C_israeli_air_force_website.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Colonel_ilan_ramon_,_israeli_air_force_website.jpg)

Ramon as a Colonel in the Israeli Air Force

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/IAF_F-16A_Netz_243_CIAF_2004.jpg/250px-IAF_F-16A_Netz_243_CIAF_2004.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:IAF_F-16A_Netz_243_CIAF_2004.jpg)

The [F-16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-16 "F-16")_Netz #243_ flown by Ramon in [Operation Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Opera "Operation Opera"). The green and black triangular emblem on the nose commemorates the attack.

Ramon was a [Colonel (_Aluf Mishne_)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Defense_Forces_ranks "Israel Defense Forces ranks") and a [fighter pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighter_aircraft "Fighter aircraft") in the [Israeli Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Air_Force "Israeli Air Force"), with thousands of hours of [flying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight "Flight") experience. He began the fighter pilot's course at the [Israeli Air Force Flight Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Air_Force_Flight_Academy "Israeli Air Force Flight Academy") in 1972, but was forced to suspend his studies after breaking his hand. Ramon served in an [electronic warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_warfare "Electronic warfare") unit in the [Sinai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinai_Peninsula "Sinai Peninsula") during the [Yom Kippur War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yom_Kippur_War "Yom Kippur War"), and afterwards, returned to the flight academy. He graduated from the fighter pilots' course in 1974. From 1974 to 1976, Ramon participated in [A-4 Skyhawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-4_Skyhawk "A-4 Skyhawk") Basic Training and Operations. From 1976 to 1980, he participated in training and operations for the [Mirage IIIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Mirage_III "Dassault Mirage III"). In 1980, as one of the IAF's establishment team of the first F-16 Squadron in Israel, Ramon attended the F-16 Training Course at [Hill Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_Air_Force_Base "Hill Air Force Base"), [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah"). From 1981 to 1983, he served as the Deputy Squadron Commander B, F-16 Squadron.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-nasabio-6)

In 1981, Ramon was the youngest pilot taking part in [Operation Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Opera "Operation Opera"), Israel's strike against [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq "Iraq")'s unfinished [Osiraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osirak "Osirak")[nuclear reactor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reactor "Nuclear reactor"). The facility was destroyed, killing ten Iraqi soldiers and one French researcher.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-8) Ramon also flew in the [1982 Lebanon War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_Lebanon_War "1982 Lebanon War").

After attending [Tel Aviv University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Aviv_University "Tel Aviv University"), Ramon served as Deputy Squadron Commander A, [119 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/119_Squadron_(Israel) "119 Squadron (Israel)"), flying the [F-4 Phantom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-4_Phantom "F-4 Phantom") (1988–1990). In 1990, he attended the Squadron Commanders Course and between 1990 and 1992, commanded [117 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/117_Squadron_(Israel) "117 Squadron (Israel)"), flying the [F-16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-16_Fighting_Falcon "F-16 Fighting Falcon"). From 1992 to 1994, Ramon was head of the Aircraft Branch in the Operations Requirement Department. In 1994, he was promoted to the rank of colonel and assigned as head of the Department of Operational Requirement for Weapon Development and Acquisition. Ramon stayed at this post until 1998.

Ramon accumulated over 3,000 flight hours on the A-4, Mirage IIIC, and F-4, and over 1,000 flight hours on the F-16.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-nasabio-6)

## NASA experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA experience")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Ilan_Ramon.jpg/250px-Ilan_Ramon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ilan_Ramon.jpg)

Ramon in November 2001

### NASA on-ground trainings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: NASA on-ground trainings")]

In 1997, Ramon was selected as a [Payload Specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Specialist "Payload Specialist"). He was designated to train as prime for a space shuttle mission with a payload that included a [multispectral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multispectral "Multispectral") camera for recording desert [aerosol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerosol "Aerosol") (dust). In July 1998, Ramon reported for training at the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston"), Texas, where he trained until 2003. Ramon flew aboard [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), logging 15 days, 22 hours and 20 minutes in space.

### Space flight: STS-107, Space Shuttle _Columbia_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Space flight: STS-107, Space Shuttle Columbia")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Ilan_ramon_sts-107.jpg/250px-Ilan_ramon_sts-107.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ilan_ramon_sts-107.jpg)

Ramon photographed aboard _Columbia_ on January 26, 2003

STS-107 _Columbia_ (January 16 – February 1, 2003), a 16-day flight, was a dedicated science and research mission. Working 24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments.

Personally nonreligious, Ramon performed traditional observance while in orbit: "I feel I am representing all Jews and all Israelis." He was the first astronaut to request [kosher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosher "Kosher") food and marked the Sabbath.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-9) Ramon, whose mother and grandmother were survivors of [Auschwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auschwitz "Auschwitz"), was asked by S. Isaac Mekel, director of development at the American Society for [Yad Vashem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yad_Vashem "Yad Vashem"), to take an item from Yad Vashem aboard STS-107. Ramon carried with him a pencil sketch, _Moon Landscape_, drawn by 16-year-old [Petr Ginz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petr_Ginz "Petr Ginz"), who was murdered in Auschwitz. Ramon also took with him a [microfiche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microfiche "Microfiche") copy of the [Torah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torah "Torah") given to him by Israeli president [Moshe Katsav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moshe_Katsav "Moshe Katsav") and a miniature Torah scroll (from the Holocaust) that was given to him by Prof. Yehoyachin Yosef, a [Bergen Belsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen_Belsen "Bergen Belsen") survivor.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-10) Ramon asked the 1939 Club, a [Holocaust survivor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_survivor "Holocaust survivor") organization in Los Angeles, for a symbol of the Holocaust to take into outer space with him. A barbed wire [mezuzah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mezuzah "Mezuzah") by the [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") artist [Aimee Golant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimee_Golant?action=edit&redlink=1 "Aimee Golant (page does not exist)") was selected. Ramon also took with him a dollar of the Lubavitcher Rebbe, Rabbi [Menachem M. Schneerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_M._Schneerson "Menachem M. Schneerson").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-11)

Ramon and the rest of the _Columbia_ crew died over East Texas in the [Southern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States") during entry into Earth's atmosphere, 16 minutes before scheduled landing.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-nasabio-6)

### Diary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Diary")]

Among the recovered 40% from the contents of the _Columbia_ Space Shuttle that broke up over Texas were 37 pages of Ramon's diary, which NASA returned to his wife.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-PC40.Wired-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-13) His widow, Rona,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-PC40.Wired-12) shared an excerpt with the Israeli public in a display at [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem "Jerusalem")'s [Israel Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Museum "Israel Museum").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-diary1-14) Rona Ramon brought it to Israel Museum [forensic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forensic "Forensic") experts. Only two pages were displayed, one containing Ramon's notes, and the other is a copy of the [Kiddush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiddush "Kiddush")[prayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prayer "Prayer").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-diary1-14)[Curator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curator "Curator")[Yigal Zalmona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yigal_Zalmona "Yigal Zalmona")[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-15) said the [diary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diary "Diary") was partially restored in one year, and needed four more, for police scientists to decipher 80% of the text. Zalmona stated: "The diary survived extreme heat in the explosion, extreme atmospheric cold, and then was attacked by microorganisms and insects. It's almost a miracle that it survived — it's incredible. There is 'no rational explanation' for how it was recovered when most of the shuttle was not."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-diary1-14) Ramon wrote on the last day of the journal:

> Today was the first day that I felt that I am truly living in space. I have become a man who lives and works in space.

Inscribed in black ink and [pencil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pencil "Pencil"), it covered the first six days of the 16-day mission.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-16)

## Family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Family")]

Ramon was survived by his wife, Rona, and their four children: Assaf, Tal, Yiftah, and Noa, who were in Florida at the time of the accident. Ramon's widow, [Rona Ramon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rona_Ramon "Rona Ramon"), served in the Israel Defense Forces as a paramedic and later earned a BA at the [Wingate Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wingate_Institute "Wingate Institute"). After Assaf's death, she returned to university and graduated with a master's degree in holistic health at [Lesley University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesley_University "Lesley University"), Massachusetts. She also lectured about dealing with grief and finding coping mechanisms. Rona served as founding CEO of the nonprofit Ramon Foundation for youth academic excellence and social leadership through science and technology.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-17) She died of pancreatic cancer on December 17, 2018.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-18) She was posthumously awarded the [Israel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Prize "Israel Prize") for lifetime achievement.

Ramon's eldest son, Assaf (February 10, 1988 – September 13, 2009), died at age 21 during a routine training flight while piloting his [F-16A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Dynamics_F-16_Fighting_Falcon "General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon"), three months after graduating from the [IAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Air_Force "Israeli Air Force") flight school [Hatzerim Airbase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatzerim_Airbase "Hatzerim Airbase") as the top cadet in his class.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-22) Assaf lost consciousness during a spell of vertigo, as a result of the high speed and G-force conditions to which he was subjected. This led to the plane crash and Assaf's subsequent death. He was considered an excellent pilot.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-Boudreaux-23) A lieutenant of the [Israeli Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Air_Force "Israeli Air Force"), he was posthumously promoted to the rank of captain.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-Boudreaux-23)

On November 10, 2013, the American Society for Yad Vashem held a special event with the participation of Ramon's son, Tal, who performed a song he wrote in memory of his father.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-JPost_2016-24) Tal Ramon performed his debut album, _Dmut_, at the club Zappa Tel Aviv in 2016.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-JPost_2016-24)

**Ilan Ramon** ([Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language"): אילן רמון; pronounced[[(ʔ)iˈlan ʁaˈmon]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Hebrew "Help:IPA/Hebrew"); June 20, 1954 – February 1, 2003)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-Stone20032-1) was an [Israeli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel")[fighter pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighter_pilot "Fighter pilot") and later the first Israeli [astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). He served as a [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") payload specialist on [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), the fatal mission of _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_, in which he and the six other crew members were killed when the spacecraft [disintegrated during re-entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"). At 48, Ramon was the oldest member of the crew. He is the first foreign recipient of the United States [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor"), which was awarded posthumously.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-2)

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Born as Ilan Wolfferman in [Ramat Gan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramat_Gan "Ramat Gan"), Israel, to Tonya (1929–2003) and Eliezer Wolfferman (1923–2006), a family of [Ashkenazi Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashkenazi_Jewish "Ashkenazi Jewish") descent, Ramon grew up in [Beersheba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beersheba "Beersheba"). His father was from [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Jews "German Jews"), and his family fled [Nazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") persecution in 1935. His mother and grandmother were from [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Jews "Polish Jews"), and were [Holocaust survivors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_survivors "Holocaust survivors"), having been in [Auschwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auschwitz "Auschwitz"). They [emigrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aliyah "Aliyah") to Israel in 1949.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-3) Ramon's first name, Ilan, means "tree" in [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-4) Ramon [Hebraizied his surname](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebraization_of_surnames "Hebraization of surnames") from **Wolfferman** to **Ramon**, a more "Israeli ([Sabra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabra_(person) "Sabra (person)"))" name, when he joined the [Israeli Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Air_Force "Israeli Air Force") (IAF). This was customary and expected of IAF pilots, as well as among [IDF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Defense_Forces "Israel Defense Forces") senior officers at the time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-5)

Ramon graduated from high school in 1972. In 1987, he graduated with a [B.Sc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in electronics and computer engineering from [Tel Aviv University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Aviv_University "Tel Aviv University").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-nasabio-6)

## Air Force career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Air Force career")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Colonel_ilan_ramon_%2C_israeli_air_force_website.jpg/250px-Colonel_ilan_ramon_%2C_israeli_air_force_website.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Colonel_ilan_ramon_,_israeli_air_force_website.jpg)

Ramon as a Colonel in the Israeli Air Force

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/IAF_F-16A_Netz_243_CIAF_2004.jpg/250px-IAF_F-16A_Netz_243_CIAF_2004.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:IAF_F-16A_Netz_243_CIAF_2004.jpg)

The [F-16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-16 "F-16")_Netz #243_ flown by Ramon in [Operation Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Opera "Operation Opera"). The green and black triangular emblem on the nose commemorates the attack.

Ramon was a [Colonel (_Aluf Mishne_)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Defense_Forces_ranks "Israel Defense Forces ranks") and a [fighter pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighter_aircraft "Fighter aircraft") in the [Israeli Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Air_Force "Israeli Air Force"), with thousands of hours of [flying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight "Flight") experience. He began the fighter pilot's course at the [Israeli Air Force Flight Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Air_Force_Flight_Academy "Israeli Air Force Flight Academy") in 1972, but was forced to suspend his studies after breaking his hand. Ramon served in an [electronic warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_warfare "Electronic warfare") unit in the [Sinai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinai_Peninsula "Sinai Peninsula") during the [Yom Kippur War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yom_Kippur_War "Yom Kippur War"), and afterwards, returned to the flight academy. He graduated from the fighter pilots' course in 1974. From 1974 to 1976, Ramon participated in [A-4 Skyhawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-4_Skyhawk "A-4 Skyhawk") Basic Training and Operations. From 1976 to 1980, he participated in training and operations for the [Mirage IIIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Mirage_III "Dassault Mirage III"). In 1980, as one of the IAF's establishment team of the first F-16 Squadron in Israel, Ramon attended the F-16 Training Course at [Hill Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_Air_Force_Base "Hill Air Force Base"), [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah"). From 1981 to 1983, he served as the Deputy Squadron Commander B, F-16 Squadron.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-nasabio-6)

In 1981, Ramon was the youngest pilot taking part in [Operation Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Opera "Operation Opera"), Israel's strike against [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq "Iraq")'s unfinished [Osiraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osirak "Osirak")[nuclear reactor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reactor "Nuclear reactor"). The facility was destroyed, killing ten Iraqi soldiers and one French researcher.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-8) Ramon also flew in the [1982 Lebanon War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_Lebanon_War "1982 Lebanon War").

After attending [Tel Aviv University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Aviv_University "Tel Aviv University"), Ramon served as Deputy Squadron Commander A, [119 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/119_Squadron_(Israel) "119 Squadron (Israel)"), flying the [F-4 Phantom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-4_Phantom "F-4 Phantom") (1988–1990). In 1990, he attended the Squadron Commanders Course and between 1990 and 1992, commanded [117 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/117_Squadron_(Israel) "117 Squadron (Israel)"), flying the [F-16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-16_Fighting_Falcon "F-16 Fighting Falcon"). From 1992 to 1994, Ramon was head of the Aircraft Branch in the Operations Requirement Department. In 1994, he was promoted to the rank of colonel and assigned as head of the Department of Operational Requirement for Weapon Development and Acquisition. Ramon stayed at this post until 1998.

Ramon accumulated over 3,000 flight hours on the A-4, Mirage IIIC, and F-4, and over 1,000 flight hours on the F-16.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-nasabio-6)

## NASA experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA experience")]

### NASA on-ground trainings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: NASA on-ground trainings")]

In 1997, Ramon was selected as a [Payload Specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payload_Specialist "Payload Specialist"). He was designated to train as prime for a space shuttle mission with a payload that included a [multispectral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multispectral "Multispectral") camera for recording desert [aerosol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerosol "Aerosol") (dust). In July 1998, Ramon reported for training at the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston"), Texas, where he trained until 2003. Ramon flew aboard [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), logging 15 days, 22 hours and 20 minutes in space.

### Space flight: STS-107, Space Shuttle _Columbia_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Space flight: STS-107, Space Shuttle Columbia")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Ilan_ramon_sts-107.jpg/250px-Ilan_ramon_sts-107.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ilan_ramon_sts-107.jpg)

Ramon photographed aboard _Columbia_ on January 26, 2003

STS-107 _Columbia_ (January 16 – February 1, 2003), a 16-day flight, was a dedicated science and research mission. Working 24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments.

Personally nonreligious, Ramon performed traditional observance while in orbit: "I feel I am representing all Jews and all Israelis." He was the first astronaut to request [kosher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosher "Kosher") food and marked the Sabbath.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-9) Ramon, whose mother and grandmother were survivors of [Auschwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auschwitz "Auschwitz"), was asked by S. Isaac Mekel, director of development at the American Society for [Yad Vashem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yad_Vashem "Yad Vashem"), to take an item from Yad Vashem aboard STS-107. Ramon carried with him a pencil sketch, _Moon Landscape_, drawn by 16-year-old [Petr Ginz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petr_Ginz "Petr Ginz"), who was murdered in Auschwitz. Ramon also took with him a [microfiche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microfiche "Microfiche") copy of the [Torah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torah "Torah") given to him by Israeli president [Moshe Katsav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moshe_Katsav "Moshe Katsav") and a miniature Torah scroll (from the Holocaust) that was given to him by Prof. Yehoyachin Yosef, a [Bergen Belsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen_Belsen "Bergen Belsen") survivor.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-10) Ramon asked the 1939 Club, a [Holocaust survivor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_survivor "Holocaust survivor") organization in Los Angeles, for a symbol of the Holocaust to take into outer space with him. A barbed wire [mezuzah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mezuzah "Mezuzah") by the [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") artist [Aimee Golant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimee_Golant?action=edit&redlink=1 "Aimee Golant (page does not exist)") was selected. Ramon also took with him a dollar of the Lubavitcher Rebbe, Rabbi [Menachem M. Schneerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_M._Schneerson "Menachem M. Schneerson").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-11)

Ramon and the rest of the _Columbia_ crew died over East Texas in the [Southern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States") during entry into Earth's atmosphere, 16 minutes before scheduled landing.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-nasabio-6)

### Diary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Diary")]

Among the recovered 40% from the contents of the _Columbia_ Space Shuttle that broke up over Texas were 37 pages of Ramon's diary, which NASA returned to his wife.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-PC40.Wired-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-13) His widow, Rona,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-PC40.Wired-12) shared an excerpt with the Israeli public in a display at [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem "Jerusalem")'s [Israel Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Museum "Israel Museum").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-diary1-14) Rona Ramon brought it to Israel Museum [forensic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forensic "Forensic") experts. Only two pages were displayed, one containing Ramon's notes, and the other is a copy of the [Kiddush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiddush "Kiddush")[prayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prayer "Prayer").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-diary1-14)[Curator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curator "Curator")[Yigal Zalmona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yigal_Zalmona "Yigal Zalmona")[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-15) said the [diary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diary "Diary") was partially restored in one year, and needed four more, for police scientists to decipher 80% of the text. Zalmona stated: "The diary survived extreme heat in the explosion, extreme atmospheric cold, and then was attacked by microorganisms and insects. It's almost a miracle that it survived — it's incredible. There is 'no rational explanation' for how it was recovered when most of the shuttle was not."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-diary1-14) Ramon wrote on the last day of the journal:

> Today was the first day that I felt that I am truly living in space. I have become a man who lives and works in space.

Inscribed in black ink and [pencil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pencil "Pencil"), it covered the first six days of the 16-day mission.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-16)

## Family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ilan_Ramon&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Family")]

Ramon was survived by his wife, Rona, and their four children: Assaf, Tal, Yiftah, and Noa, who were in Florida at the time of the accident. Ramon's widow, [Rona Ramon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rona_Ramon "Rona Ramon"), served in the Israel Defense Forces as a paramedic and later earned a BA at the [Wingate Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wingate_Institute "Wingate Institute"). After Assaf's death, she returned to university and graduated with a master's degree in holistic health at [Lesley University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesley_University "Lesley University"), Massachusetts. She also lectured about dealing with grief and finding coping mechanisms. Rona served as founding CEO of the nonprofit Ramon Foundation for youth academic excellence and social leadership through science and technology.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-17) She died of pancreatic cancer on December 17, 2018.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-18) She was posthumously awarded the [Israel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Prize "Israel Prize") for lifetime achievement.

Ramon's eldest son, Assaf (February 10, 1988 – September 13, 2009), died at age 21 during a routine training flight while piloting his [F-16A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Dynamics_F-16_Fighting_Falcon "General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon"), three months after graduating from the [IAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Air_Force "Israeli Air Force") flight school [Hatzerim Airbase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatzerim_Airbase "Hatzerim Airbase") as the top cadet in his class.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-22) Assaf lost consciousness during a spell of vertigo, as a result of the high speed and G-force conditions to which he was subjected. This led to the plane crash and Assaf's subsequent death. He was considered an excellent pilot.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-Boudreaux-23) A lieutenant of the [Israeli Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Air_Force "Israeli Air Force"), he was posthumously promoted to the rank of captain.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-Boudreaux-23)

On November 10, 2013, the American Society for Yad Vashem held a special event with the participation of Ramon's son, Tal, who performed a song he wrote in memory of his father.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-JPost_2016-24) Tal Ramon performed his debut album, _Dmut_, at the club Zappa Tel Aviv in 2016.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Ramon#cite_note-JPost_2016-24)

**Laurel Blair Clark** (née **Salton**; March 10, 1961 – February 1, 2003) was an American [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") astronaut, medical doctor, [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy")[captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(U.S._Navy) "Captain (U.S. Navy)"), and [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission specialist. She died along with her six fellow crew members in the [Space Shuttle _Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster"). Clark was posthumously awarded the [Congressional Space Medal of Honor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Space_Medal_of_Honor "Congressional Space Medal of Honor").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Clark was born in [Ames, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ames,_Iowa "Ames, Iowa"), but considered [Racine, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racine,_Wisconsin "Racine, Wisconsin"), her hometown. She graduated from [William Horlick High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Horlick_High_School "William Horlick High School") in [Racine, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racine,_Wisconsin "Racine, Wisconsin") in 1979. She enrolled at the [University of Wisconsin–Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin%E2%80%93Madison "University of Wisconsin–Madison"), where she received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [zoology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoology "Zoology") in 1983, and a [Doctor of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine "Doctor of Medicine") in 1987. Clark was also a member of the [Gamma Phi Beta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_Phi_Beta "Gamma Phi Beta") sorority at the university. She held a [Federal Communications Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission "Federal Communications Commission") (FCC) issued Technician Class [amateur radio license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_radio_license "Amateur radio license") with the [call sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_sign "Call sign") KC5ZSU.

## Military career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career")]

During medical school, Clark did active duty training with the Diving Medicine Department at the [United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_Experimental_Diving_Unit "United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit") in March 1987. After completing medical school, she underwent postgraduate medical education in pediatrics from 1987 to 1988 at the [National Naval Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Naval_Medical_Center "National Naval Medical Center"). The following year, Clark completed Navy undersea medical officer training at the Naval Undersea Medical Institute in [Groton, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groton,_Connecticut "Groton, Connecticut"), and diving medical officer training at the Naval Diving and Salvage Training Center in [Panama City, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_City,_Florida "Panama City, Florida"). She was designated a Radiation Health Officer and Undersea Medical Officer. Clark was then assigned as the [Submarine Squadron 14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Submarine_Squadron_14 "Submarine Squadron 14") Medical Department Head in [Holy Loch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Loch "Holy Loch"), Scotland. During that assignment, she dove with Navy divers and [Naval Special Warfare Unit Two SEALs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_SEALs "United States Navy SEALs") and performed many medical evacuations from US submarines. After two years of operational experience, Clark was designated as a Naval Submarine Medical Officer and Diving Medical Officer.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-NASAbio-1)

Clark underwent six months of aeromedical training at the Naval Aerospace Medical Institute at [NAS Pensacola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAS_Pensacola "NAS Pensacola") in [Pensacola, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pensacola,_Florida "Pensacola, Florida"), and was designated as a Naval Flight Surgeon. She was stationed at [MCAS Yuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MCAS_Yuma "MCAS Yuma"), [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona "Arizona"), and assigned as Flight Surgeon Marine Attack Squadron 211 (VMA-211), a Marine Corps [AV-8B Harrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AV-8B_Harrier "AV-8B Harrier") squadron. Clark made several deployments, including one overseas to the Western Pacific, practiced medicine in austere environments, and flew on multiple aircraft. Her squadron won the Marine Attack Squadron of the Year award for its successful deployment. Clark was then assigned as the Group Flight Surgeon for [Marine Aircraft Group 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Aircraft_Group_13 "Marine Aircraft Group 13") (MAG-13).

Before her selection as an astronaut candidate, Clark served as a Flight Surgeon for Training Squadron 86 ([VT-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VT-86 "VT-86")), the [Naval Flight Officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Flight_Officer "Naval Flight Officer") advanced training squadron for tactical jets at NAS Pensacola. She was Board Certified by the National Board of Medical Examiners and held a Wisconsin Medical License, and her military qualifications included Radiation Health Officer, Undersea Medical Officer, Diving Medical Officer, Submarine Medical Officer, and Naval Flight Surgeon. Clark was also a Basic Life Support Instructor, Advanced Cardiac Life Support Provider, Advanced Trauma Life Support Provider, and Hyperbaric Chamber Advisor. Clark was a member of the [Aerospace Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_Medical_Association "Aerospace Medical Association") and the Society of U.S. Naval Flight Surgeons.

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Selected by NASA in April 1996, Clark reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in [Houston, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston,_Texas "Houston, Texas"), in August 1996.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-2) After completing two years of training and evaluation, she was qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist. From July 1997 to August 2000, Clark worked in the Astronaut Office Payloads/Habitability Branch. She flew aboard [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107"), logging 15 days, 22 hours and 21 minutes in space.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-NASAbio-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-3)

### Space flight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Space flight experience")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/LaurelClarkSTS107.jpg/250px-LaurelClarkSTS107.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LaurelClarkSTS107.jpg)

Laurel Clark during STS-107

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/STS-107_Laurel_Clark.jpg/250px-STS-107_Laurel_Clark.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-107_Laurel_Clark.jpg)

Laurel Clark looks through an overhead window on the aft flight deck of the Shuttle.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-4)

Main article: [STS-107](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-107 "STS-107")

STS-107 _Columbia_ – The 16-day flight was a dedicated science and research mission. Working 24 hours a day, in two alternating shifts, the crew successfully conducted approximately 80 experiments. Clark's bioscience experiments included gardening in space, as she discussed only days before her death in an interview with [Milwaukee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee "Milwaukee") media near her Wisconsin hometown. The STS-107 mission ended abruptly on February 1, 2003, when _Columbia_ disintegrated and her crew perished during re-entry, 16 minutes before scheduled landing.

Clark also recorded inside the cockpit during _Columbia_'s descent into the Earth's atmosphere on a small digital camera.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-5)

Clark's final message to her friends and family was through an email sent from _Columbia_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-7) In the released text of the email, Clark called the planet magnificent, and explained that while she spends much of the time working back in Spacehab and away from the sights of Earth, "whenever I do get to look out, it is glorious." Clark found that taking photos of the Earth was challenging, "Keeping my fingers crossed that they're in sharp focus." Clark also shared some of the intriguing effects of micro gravity on human physiology, such as constant challenge to stay adequately hydrated due to an "almost non-existent" sense of thirst.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-8)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Clark is survived by her husband, fellow former U.S. Navy captain and NASA flight surgeon Dr. Jonathan Clark (who was part of an official NASA panel that prepared the final 400-page report about the _Columbia_ disaster), and son Iain who was born in 1996.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-10) She was also a member of the Olympia Brown Unitarian Universalist Church in Racine, Wisconsin.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-11)

## Tributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laurel_Clark&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tributes")]

*   [Asteroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid "Asteroid")[51827 Laurelclark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51827_Laurelclark "51827 Laurelclark") was named for Clark.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-12)
*   Clark Hill in the [Columbia Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Hills_(Mars) "Columbia Hills (Mars)") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") was named for Clark.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-13)
*   L. Clark, an interior crater of the lunar crater [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_(crater) "Apollo (crater)"), was named for Clark.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-15)
*   Clark Hall, in the Columbia Village Suites at the [Florida Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Institute_of_Technology "Florida Institute of Technology"), is named after her.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The apartments were initially planned to be named the Crane Creek Suites, but were renamed in 2008 to commemorate the _Columbia_ crew.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   The Laurel Salton Clark Memorial Fountain in Racine, Wisconsin is named for her.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-16)
*   In 2004, the Naval Aerospace Medicine Institute named its Aerospace Medicine Academic Center in [Pensacola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pensacola "Pensacola") after Clark and David M. Brown[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-17)
*   Clark Auditorium at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, Bethesda, Maryland is named for her and displays uniforms, training manuals, and personal items that belonged to her.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-18)
*   The Scottish band [Runrig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runrig "Runrig") pays tribute to Clark on the 2016 album _[The Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Story\_(Runrig\_album) "The Story (Runrig album)")_. The final track, "Somewhere", ends with a recording of her voice.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-19) Clark was a Runrig fan and had a wake up call with Runrig's "Running to the Light". She took their 2001 _[The Stamping Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Stamping\_Ground "The Stamping Ground")_ CD into space with her. When the shuttle disintegrated the CD was found among the debris that reached the Earth's surface, and was presented to the band by her family.
*   [Northrop Grumman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northrop_Grumman "Northrop Grumman") named a [Cygnus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cygnus_(spacecraft) "Cygnus (spacecraft)") cargo spacecraft [S.S. _Laurel Clark_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cygnus_NG-19 "Cygnus NG-19").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Clark#cite_note-20)
